clue.text: Join second force, having nothing to lose

indicators.note: to lose means the force gives up the round letter for nothing

parts.note: the police are often called the force
O, shaped like zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: Advice to someone joining a second army or police force with nothing to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'force' looks like strength, but it is the police; 'to lose' drops its O.
explanation.definitionFit: To splice ropes or film is to unite two ends together.

clue.text: Incite single girl to become wanton

parts.note: to prod is to urge or incite
I, the Roman one, means single
gal is an informal word for girl

explanation.surface: Encouraging a single girl to become promiscuous.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigal means recklessly extravagant, as wanton spending is.

clue.text: Money paid in a note to others

parts.note: taken as written
te is a note of the sol-fa scale
the rest means the others

explanation.surface: Cash sent along with a covering note to other people.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest is the charge levied on a loan by the lender.

clue.text: Remove cycle with heartless order

parts.note: an era is a cycle or age

indicators.note: heartless means losing the middle letter of the word for order

parts.note: to dictate is to order

explanation.surface: Getting rid of a bicycle with a cruel command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes only the middle letter of the order word; 'cycle' is an age, not a bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: To eradicate is to root out or destroy completely.

clue.text: Excessive number involved in forgery of voucher

indicators.note: the number is wrapped up inside the rearranged letters
a forgery is a fake made up, so the word voucher is reworked into a new order

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a number

explanation.surface: A fraudster forges a voucher for an excessive sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgery of' rearranges the letters of 'voucher', and 'involved in' sets the Roman thousand among them.
explanation.definitionFit: Overmuch is an adjective for too great in amount or degree.

clue.text: Hash or stew fifth-rate? Quite the reverse!

indicators.note: making a hash of the words means jumbling them into a new order

explanation.surface: A cook's stew is judged fifth-rate, then praised as excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hash' sounds like the dish but rearranges OR STEW FIFTH-RATE; the definition points back at fifth-rate, whose opposite is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the first water describes a gem of the purest lustre, so of top quality, the opposite of mediocre.

clue.text: Back to sea with new weaponry

parts.note: the rear is the back
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A navy returns to sea newly armed.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearmed means equipped again with arms.

clue.text: Explosive blows up rock out of bed at first eruption

indicators.note: at first places the out-of-bed word at the front

parts.note: someone up is out of bed
HE is short for high explosive

indicators.note: in a down clue, blows up sends the rock upwards, reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: lava is molten rock that sets solid

explanation.surface: A volcano blasts rock upward, waking everyone at the first eruption.
explanation.walkthrough: As held, the clue had the next clue's text run on; the page ends at 'eruption'. In a down entry 'blows up' turns the rock upwards, and 'at first' sends the out-of-bed word to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: An upheaval is a violent heaving up of the earth's crust, or any sudden disruption.

clue.text: Merriment — it makes an appearance during term

indicators.note: turning up during a period means sitting inside the word for that term

parts.note: Hilary is the spring term at Oxford University and in the English law courts
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fun breaks out partway through a school term.
explanation.walkthrough: HILARY is the January-to-March term at Oxford and in the English courts.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilarity is loud laughter and high spirits.

clue.text: Catch game

definitions.meaning: ... bridge is the card game usually just called bridge

explanation.definitionFit: Contracting a disease is catching it, and contract is the bridge variant played at most card tables.

clue.text: Artist from Harlow

indicators.note: the artist is made from the letters of the town name, rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter who comes from the Essex new town of Harlow.
explanation.walkthrough: HARLOW, a new town in Essex, rearranges to give the American pop artist; 'from' is an unusually quiet anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Andy Warhol was the American pop painter of soup cans and Marilyn prints.

clue.text: Married to Arthur's mother — what a headache!

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married in genealogy and forms
in Arthurian legend King Arthur's mother is Igraine

explanation.surface: Someone groans at being wed to King Arthur's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a mother-in-law joke, but IGRAINE is simply Arthur's mother from the legends, after M for married.
explanation.definitionFit: A migraine is a severe recurring pain in the head, the archetypal bad headache.

clue.text: One thousand and two hurt

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
a pair is two of something

explanation.surface: A tally of casualties: a thousand and two people hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to damage or weaken it.

clue.text: Iberian resort about empty

parts.note: a spa is a health resort

indicators.note: about signals turning the word for empty round

parts.note: to empty a tank is to drain it

explanation.surface: A Spanish seaside resort lies about empty out of season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' but turns the word for empty back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spaniard is a native of Spain, on the Iberian peninsula.

clue.text: Concerned with fool about to eat what is being prepared?

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: about means the word for fool goes round the eating word

parts.note: an ass is a fool
to dine is to eat

explanation.surface: A worried question about a fool about to eat the food being made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sounds like 'on the point of' but is the container signal; the definition's question mark flags its cryptic slant.
explanation.definitionFit: Readiness is the state of being fully set up and prepared.

clue.text: To fly, fellow gets drunk

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS
lit is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A man gets drunk before catching a flight.
explanation.definitionFit: To flit is to move lightly and swiftly, like a bird or moth darting.

clue.text: Fools fasten flap

parts.note: a flat is old slang for a dupe or fool
to pin something is to fasten it

explanation.surface: Fools are pinning down a loose flap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flap' here is not a loose piece but a state of panic.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat spin is a state of agitated panic, like a dither.

clue.text: With winter coming, the telephone plays a vital part

indicators.note: the answer forms an internal part of the phrase winter coming

explanation.surface: In winter the telephone becomes essential for keeping in touch.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across wINTER COMing.
explanation.definitionFit: An intercom is an internal telephone system linking rooms in a building.

clue.text: Marble accessory

definitions.meaning: an ... or alley is a large glass or alabaster playing marble
in law an accessory is one who helps a criminal, a confederate

explanation.definitionFit: A child's alley-taw is a fine playing marble, and a partner in crime is a confederate.

clue.text: Tree I saw moving, so to speak

indicators.note: the letters are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A Macbeth-like vision of a tree walking, figuratively speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: As it were is the phrase that hedges a figure of speech, like in a manner of speaking.

clue.text: To have a good time. I have started smoking outside

indicators.note: outside means the smoking words go round the contraction

parts.note: to light up is to start a cigarette
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A partygoer's confession that they took up smoking.
explanation.walkthrough: LIT UP goes round I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Living it up is the idiom for enjoying oneself lavishly.

clue.text: Get dazed and stop talking to sailors

indicators.note: talking means we take what the word for stop sounds like when spoken

parts.note: to stop is to cease
tars is old slang for sailors

explanation.surface: An order to cut out the chatter to the ship's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: CEASE said out loud gives SEES; add TARS for sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing stars is the idiom for being dazed by a blow to the head.

clue.text: In a way, foreigner is striking

indicators.note: in places the foreigner inside the word for way

parts.note: St, for street, is a way
an alien is a foreigner

explanation.surface: An outsider's appearance is in a way striking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a way' reads as a hedge, but 'In' is the container signal and 'way' the street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A salient feature is prominent or conspicuous.

clue.text: Voice is a hit in this circle

definitions.meaning: a high singing voice, typically a boy's
on a dartboard, a dart landing in the narrow inner ring scores triple

explanation.walkthrough: THIS circle is the dartboard's inner ring; a dart landing there is called by the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest boy's singing part shares its name with the dartboard ring that triples a score.

clue.text: I left Wiltshire to be trained as an artist

indicators.note: left means the I is taken away from the county name
trained in the sense of reshaped, so the remaining letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone leaves the county of Wiltshire to study art.
explanation.walkthrough: WILTSHIRE is an English county; 'I left' takes out an I and 'to be trained' rearranges the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: James McNeill Whistler was the American-born painter famous for his portrait of his mother.

clue.text: Pale people demonstrating

definitions.meaning: a pale is a pointed stake in a fence
strikers standing outside a workplace in protest form a line

explanation.definitionFit: A pointed fence stake shares its name with a line of strikers outside a factory gate.

clue.text: Modern incursion into the 14th century

indicators.note: an incursion is a push in, so the word for modern goes in, the 'in' of into, leaving to as the host

parts.note: the word into splits as in plus to, and to supplies the outer letters
recent means modern

explanation.surface: Modern life forcing its way into a medieval period.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints '14th', not '4th'. The setter reads 'incursion into' as the modern word going in 'to', the last two letters of 'into' wrapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trecento is the Italian term for the 1300s, especially in art history.

clue.text: Talk about order — it is unimportant

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the chat word surrounds the order

parts.note: to natter is to chat or talk idly
OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour

explanation.surface: Gossip about a command, dismissed as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Order of Merit is a British honour; 'about' has the chat word going round its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying no matter means the thing makes no difference, so is of little consequence.

clue.text: Plain speaking of course

indicators.note: speaking means we take what the plain's name sounds like when spoken

parts.note: each stage of a course of action or study is a step

explanation.surface: A remark about speaking plainly, of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain speaking' looks like a phrase for frankness; Plain is the definition and 'speaking' the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A steppe is a vast treeless grassland plain, as in Central Asia.
